overview.text: Switzerland, officially the Swiss Confederation, is a landlocked country in Central Europe with three major geographical regions: the Alps, the Central Plateau and the Jura. The Alps cover much of the country, while the plateau contains many of its populated areas. Political power is shared among the Confederation, 26 cantons and communes; cantons have their own constitutions and governments, making federalism a defining feature. Switzerland’s four national languages—German, French, Italian and Romansh—reflect its regional diversity. Although the name “Swiss Confederation” is retained for historical reasons, Switzerland has been a federal state since 1848.

key_facts.text: Switzerland has no coastline and borders five countries: Italy, France, Germany, Austria and Liechtenstein.
Its three main geographical regions are the Alps, Central Plateau and Jura; the plateau has the highest concentration of populated areas.
The 26 cantons have their own constitutions, parliaments and governments, and share political power with the national Confederation and communes.
German, French, Italian and Romansh are the four national languages; Romansh is used for official federal purposes in Romansh-speaking areas.
The name “Swiss Confederation” is historical: Switzerland has been a federal state since 1848. The name’s origin is associated with a founding legend.
